current: Whether form controls have a programmatic label (an associated label, aria-label or aria-labelledby), buttons have text, links have an accessible name, a click handler on a plain element names the control it declares, fieldsets have a non-empty legend, known UI-library field components carry a label prop, and a placeholder isn't used as the only label. Static markup readiness, not a WCAG conformance claim.
proposed: Whether form fields (for example text inputs, selects and text areas) have a programmatic label (a label element associated with the field by reference or by wrapping it, aria-label or aria-labelledby), buttons have an accessible name (text content, aria-label or aria-labelledby), links have an accessible name, a non-interactive element (for example a div or span) that has a click handler and declares a control role gives that control an accessible name, fieldsets have a non-empty legend, a field component that takes its label through a property (for example a UI library's text-field component with a label prop) is given that property, and a placeholder is not used as the only label. A reading of the markup as written in source, not of the rendered page; not a WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) conformance claim.

current: Whether interactive behaviour is keyboard-reachable — no click handler on a non-interactive element lacking a role, tabindex and key handler, no element the repo's own CSS styles `cursor: pointer` without giving it any of the three, no unfocusable element whose only binding is a mouse enter/leave pair or a double-click, no positive tabindex, no href-less anchor, no placeholder-href (#/javascript) link acting as a button. Static markup readiness, not a WCAG conformance claim.
proposed: Whether interactive behaviour can be reached and used from the keyboard: a non-interactive element (one with no native control behaviour, for example a div or span) that has a click handler has an accessibility role, a tab index and a keyboard handler; an element the repository's own style sheets give a pointer cursor has at least one of those three; an element whose only event handlers are a mouse enter/leave pair or a double-click can receive focus; no element has a positive tab index; no anchor lacks an href; and no link whose href is a placeholder (an empty fragment or a script URL, for example '#' or 'javascript:') acts as a button, that is, performs an action instead of navigating, through a click handler or through the script URL itself. A reading of the markup and styles as written in source, not of the running page; not a WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) conformance claim.

current: Whether focus outlines aren't removed without a replacement, motion respects prefers-reduced-motion, and literal CSS colour pairs meet contrast — PARTIAL: inline styles, in-repo <style> blocks, in-repo .css files, var() tokens, Tailwind neutral utilities and CSS-in-JS literals are read (hex/rgb/hsl/named), never computed/runtime/external-CDN colour. Static markup readiness, not a WCAG conformance claim.
proposed: Whether focus outlines are not removed without a replacement focus style, motion (for example animations and transitions) is conditioned on the user's reduced-motion preference, and colour pairs written as literal values in the repository's own styles (including style tokens and utility classes that resolve to literal colours) meet a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Colours computed at runtime or loaded from outside the repository are not assessed. Static markup readiness, not a WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) conformance claim.

current: How the codebase splits by code ROLE — domain, application, infrastructure, test, generated. The significance map behind the knowledge/coupling weighting, and a DDD signal in its own right: a thin domain core under fat infrastructure is the anemic-domain smell, quantified.
proposed: How the code divides, by size, among five roles, each piece of code having one: domain (the code that models the business and holds its rules), application (the code that carries out use cases by directing the domain), infrastructure (the code that connects to the outside world, for example databases, networks, files and frameworks), test (the code that tests other code) and generated (code produced by a tool rather than written by hand). In domain-driven design terms, a small domain share beside a large infrastructure share suggests an anemic domain model, one whose types hold data while the business rules live elsewhere. A split by size, not proof of where the behaviour lives.

current: The Runtime Evidence tier found no declared way to boot this app (docker-compose, Aspire AppHost, or a Dockerfile), so no live runtime a11y/egress/header evidence was gathered. Advisory — never affects the CAI score.
proposed: Whether the repository declares a way to boot the application: a compose file (with one service or several, for example a docker-compose file), an orchestration project that starts the application and its services (for example a .NET Aspire AppHost), or a container build file (for example a Dockerfile). The finding is raised when none is declared: then no evidence is gathered from the running application for the dimensions observed on it (rendered accessibility, outbound requests and security headers), though those dimensions may still have evidence from reading the code. A declared way to boot is not proof that the application builds or boots. Advisory: it explains missing runtime evidence and is never counted in any CAI score.

current: HTTP security headers the live app actually set, observed by booting it in our no-coupling sandbox — advisory evidence for AppSec / CRA / NIS2 runtime secure-defaults. Never scored.
proposed: Which HTTP security headers the running application actually sets in its responses (for example Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy or Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy), observed while the application runs, never inferred from source. A header counts as set when a response carries it: the result records presence, not whether a value is strong (a policy that allows inline scripts still counts as set), and a deployment configured otherwise may send other headers. Advisory evidence for application security, for the secure-by-default requirements of the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and for the cybersecurity risk-management measures of the NIS2 Directive; never counted in any CAI score.

current: WCAG success criteria verified in a real headless-browser render (axe-core), double-render checked and kept as advisory evidence — never scored.
proposed: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) success criteria checked on the page as a browser renders it, including those only a rendered page can show (for example contrast as displayed, focus order, and state that exists only once the page runs). A result counts only when it is reproducible: the same page rendered again gives the same result. Not a WCAG conformance claim: automated checks on a rendered page cover only part of the success criteria. Advisory: failures are reported as findings, never counted in any CAI score, and never change the static accessibility dimensions (AC1-AC6, which read the source without running it).

current: Every network binding the application actually opened when booted in our no-coupling sandbox — service, container port, host port, protocol and bind scope — with any port the repository's own files never declare called out. Observed, never inferred from a manifest. Advisory; never scored.
proposed: Every network binding the application actually opens when the stack the repository declares is started as declared, each with its service, container port, host port, protocol and bind scope (the addresses the port listens on, for example all interfaces or the local machine only), with any port the repository's own files never declare called out, for example one a base image opens. A port counts as declared when a file of the repository names it, for example a compose file's port mappings or a container build file's exposed ports. The bindings themselves are observed on the running application, never taken from those files, which serve only to tell declared ports from undeclared ones. An inventory, not a risk verdict: it does not say which networks can reach a port. Advisory: reported as evidence, never counted in any CAI score.

current: Whether any dependency has a known published vulnerability (CVE), direct or transitive, in ANY ecosystem the repository declares — Dart pub, Elixir and Erlang via Hex, Go modules, Java and Kotlin via Maven/Gradle, JavaScript/npm, .NET/NuGet, PHP/Composer, Python/PyPI, RubyGems, Rust/Cargo and Swift.
proposed: Whether any dependency of the repository, direct or transitive, in any package ecosystem the repository declares (for example npm, PyPI, Maven or Cargo), is affected at the version in use by a known published vulnerability, as recorded in a security advisory (for example a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entry or a GHSA (GitHub Security Advisory) entry). A match of the version in use against the advisories known at the time of reading: not proof that the vulnerable code is reached or exploitable, and no match does not mean the dependencies are free of vulnerabilities.

current: Whether the build pipeline provides supply-chain integrity — generated provenance/attestation, signed artifacts (cosign/sigstore), an SBOM, and pinned build actions. Presence of the configuration, not a runtime guarantee.
proposed: Whether the build pipeline, including the configuration that publishes its releases, provides supply-chain integrity: generated provenance or attestation (a record, often signed, of how and from what an artifact was built), signed artifacts, an SBOM (software bill of materials, a machine-readable list of the components in an artifact), and build actions the pipeline reuses (for example CI actions or included templates) pinned to an immutable reference, such as a full commit hash or digest, rather than a movable tag or branch. Presence of the configuration, not a runtime guarantee.

current: Whether the Kubernetes deployment wires runtime threat enforcement — a detection engine (Tetragon/Falco) and/or an admission-control policy gate (Kyverno / OPA Gatekeeper / PodSecurity). Presence of committed policy, not a runtime guarantee.
proposed: Whether the Kubernetes deployment commits runtime threat controls: a threat-detection engine that watches running workloads and alerts on suspicious behaviour, and/or an admission-control policy that rejects non-compliant workloads when they are deployed (for example Falco or Tetragon for detection; Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper or Pod Security admission for admission control). Presence of committed policy, not a runtime guarantee.

current: Whether any dependency the repository declares is published as MALICIOUS rather than merely vulnerable — a package that is an attacker's work, in any ecosystem osv-scanner reads. Reported apart from D30 because the answer is binary: there is no safe version to upgrade to, and the fix is to remove the package and rotate every credential it could have read.
proposed: Whether any dependency the repository declares, in any ecosystem, is published as malicious rather than merely vulnerable: recorded by a vulnerability or malicious-package database as an attacker's work (for example an entry in the OpenSSF malicious-packages feed, or an advisory classified as embedded malicious code). Reported apart from Dependency Vulnerabilities (D30) because there is no safe version to upgrade to: the package must be removed and every credential it could have read rotated.

current: Whether entities protect their state (private/init-only setters) instead of exposing public setters that bypass invariants. Softened when a rehydration framework (Marten/EF) is present.
proposed: Whether entities (domain objects with an identity whose rules, or invariants, they must keep) protect their state, writable only inside the entity or when it is constructed, instead of exposing publicly writable state that bypasses those invariants, such as public setters or the entity's own mutable collections handed out directly rather than as a copy or read-only view. Softened where the code uses a persistence framework that rebuilds entities from stored state (for example Entity Framework or Marten).

current: Whether the domain layer stays free of infrastructure dependencies (EF/Marten/HTTP/ASP.NET) — the clean-architecture dependency rule.
proposed: Whether the domain layer (the code that holds the business rules) stays free of infrastructure dependencies, for example persistence, database or cache clients, HTTP clients, web-framework or message-bus types: the clean-architecture dependency rule, that inner domain code never depends on outer infrastructure code.

current: Whether Apply/When folds reconstruct state purely from the event (no DateTime.Now, Guid.NewGuid, Random or IO) so replay is reproducible.
proposed: In event-sourced code, whether the functions that rebuild state from each stored event (event folds, for example in aggregates or projections, often named Apply or When) compute the new state only from the prior state and the event: without reading the current time, drawing a random number, generating a new identifier or doing I/O (input or output, for example reading a file, a database or the network). This is what makes replaying the same events always give the same state.

current: Unreviewed-generation residue: shipped members still throwing NotImplementedException, and placeholder string literals left in non-test, non-generated code. Scored as a quality signature, never as a claim about authorship.
proposed: Leftovers of unfinished code (for example scaffolding, or AI coding-assistant output never completed) in production code, excluding tests and code emitted by a code generator (for example files marked as auto-generated): code that still throws an error marking it as not yet implemented (for example NotImplementedException in .NET), and placeholder string literals, that is, literals whose text stands in for real content still to be written (for example "TODO", "lorem ipsum", "changeme" or "your-api-key-here"). Scored on what the code shows, as a quality signal, never as a claim about who or what wrote it.

current: Unfinished work detected by code SHAPE, not keywords: members that only throw a "not implemented" exception, methods that take inputs and return a constant, async methods that never await, dead `if (false)` / `#if false` branches, and skeleton types most of whose members are holes. A real, objective slice of technical debt.
proposed: Unfinished work recognised by the shape of the code, not by keywords such as TODO: members that only throw a not-implemented error, methods that take inputs and return a constant, asynchronous methods that never wait on anything, code disabled by a constant false condition in source or in conditional compilation (for example `if (false)` or `#if false`), and skeleton types most of whose members are unfinished in one of these ways.

current: Whether database schema changes go through versioned migrations rather than being auto-created from the model (EF Core EnsureCreated(), GORM AutoMigrate, SQLAlchemy create_all, TypeORM synchronize, Hibernate ddl-auto).
proposed: Whether database schema changes in production code and configuration go through versioned migrations (a committed, ordered history of schema changes) rather than being created or altered automatically from the application's entity or model definitions (for example EF Core EnsureCreated, GORM AutoMigrate, SQLAlchemy create_all, TypeORM synchronize set to true, Hibernate ddl-auto set to create or update). Test code, for example a fixture that creates a throwaway database, is excluded. A positive result means production schema changes are recorded as versioned migrations and not created automatically; it is not proof that the migrations are applied or match the live schema.

current: Whether test coverage concentrates on the domain (business rules) rather than the trivial web/controller layer — a focus check a generic tool can't make.
proposed: Whether test coverage falls on the domain layer (the business rules) rather than on the web or controller layer, the code that receives requests and hands them to the domain and should hold little logic of its own.

current: Whether asynchronous code stays responsive — it avoids sync-over-async blocking (a .NET .Wait()/.GetAwaiter().GetResult(), a time.sleep or blocking HTTP call inside a Python coroutine, a *Sync call inside an async JavaScript function, block_on inside a Rust async fn, runBlocking inside a Kotlin suspend function, block() inside a Reactor publisher) that stalls a thread or event loop and risks deadlock, and, where the code is a reusable library on .NET, awaits with ConfigureAwait(false) so it never captures and stalls its caller's context.
proposed: Whether asynchronous work in production code (tests excluded) is kept from blocking a thread or event loop. Two things count. First, a synchronous wait for asynchronous work to finish (sync-over-async): in .NET anywhere in production code, not only inside async methods (for example .Wait() or .GetAwaiter().GetResult() on a task), because a blocked thread can deadlock the very work it waits for; in other languages where the wait sits inside asynchronous code (for example block_on in a Rust async function, runBlocking in a Kotlin suspend function, or block() inside a reactive publisher). Second, a blocking call made inside asynchronous code (for example a blocking sleep or HTTP call inside a Python coroutine, or a synchronous file call inside an async JavaScript function). Either stalls a thread or loop and risks deadlock. And where the code is a reusable .NET library (code packaged for other applications to use), its awaits do not resume on the caller's captured context (for example by using ConfigureAwait(false)), so the library does not deadlock or stall a caller that blocks on it.

current: Per-function cyclomatic/cognitive complexity from the token-level function scanner (D-386) — real branching, not a regex heuristic.
proposed: Per-function complexity of the frontend code, counted from each function's actual branching: cyclomatic complexity, one plus each decision point (a condition, a loop, a case label or a short-circuit boolean operator); and cognitive complexity, one increment for each if, else-if, else, conditional expression, switch, loop, catch, labelled jump, recursive call and run of the same boolean operator, plus, for the structures that nest (conditionals, conditional expressions, switches, loops and catches), one more for each level of nesting they sit in.

current: Static test reachability (D-386): the share of production files reachable from any test via the import graph — measured without running anything.
proposed: Static test reachability: the share of production files that at least one test reaches by following imports, directly or through other imported files, found without running anything. It is not runtime line or branch coverage.

current: Whether the project wires up test, lint and typecheck — detected from each package.json script's COMMAND (eslint / tsc / vitest / jest / playwright), not just its name, and corroborated against CI-workflow invocations so a tool run only in CI still counts.
proposed: Whether the project wires up each of test, lint and type-check runs: in a package.json script, judged by the command the script runs (for example eslint, tsc, vitest, jest or playwright) rather than by its name, so a script named test that runs no test tool does not count; or in a CI (continuous integration) workflow that invokes such a tool, so a tool run only in CI also counts. The presence of that wiring, not evidence that the checks run or pass.

current: Files unreachable from every application/tooling/test entry point, and exports nothing imports (module-graph reachability, D-386).
proposed: Dead code: files that cannot be reached by following imports, directly or through other files, from any entry point (an application start file, a tooling or configuration file, or a test), and exports that no file in the repository imports. Tests count as entry points, not as candidates. A file loaded only by a framework convention rather than an import (for example a route file found by its folder) can appear here, so a finding is not proof that the file is unused.

current: npm dependency truthfulness (D-386): unused dependencies, imports not declared anywhere, and type-/test-only packages shipped as production deps.
proposed: Whether an npm package's declared dependencies match what its code uses: dependencies its package.json declares that the code does not use, packages the code imports (by any form of loading, for example import or require) that are not declared anywhere, and packages needed only for types or tests (for example @types packages or a test runner) declared as production dependencies rather than development dependencies. Built-in runtime modules and relative imports of the package's own files are not packages. Not a check of whether dependencies are outdated, vulnerable or licensed.

current: Import cycles in the module graph (D-386) — files that can only be understood and changed together.
proposed: Import cycles in the module graph of the frontend code (the code of the user interface that runs in the browser or another client): source files that import each other in a loop, directly (two files importing each other) or through others (A imports B, B imports C, C imports A), so they can only be understood and changed together.

current: The share of the scored frontend lines inside a near-exact copy-pasted block of substantial extent (the D4 clone algorithm over JS/TS tokens, D-386; each line once, 10 at none and 0 at a quarter of the lines, as D4): a block is reported only where its copies still agree on most of their own identifiers and literals, or were renamed as they were pasted but kept most of their constants, and where the copies carry enough code to stand on their own or the copied extent reaches 30 lines — so a re-implementation sharing neither names nor values, and a small pasted declaration, are both found and deliberately not reported, and a clean R10 is not a claim that nothing was copied.
proposed: The share of the frontend code's production lines inside a near-exact copy-pasted block of substantial extent, each line counted once. A copied block counts where its copies still agree on most of their own identifiers and literal values, or were renamed as they were pasted but kept most of their constants; and where, in addition, the copies either carry enough code to stand on their own (more than a small declaration such as a list of fields or imports) or the copied extent reaches 30 lines. The exact shares and minimum size are stated on the dimension page. A re-implementation sharing neither names nor values, and a small pasted declaration, are not counted, so a clean R10 (no such block found) is not a claim that nothing was copied.

current: Conformance to the detected frontend architecture layout (feature-sliced / layered src) plus cross-package deep-import rules (D-386).
proposed: Whether imports in the frontend code respect the boundaries of the architecture layout the code follows, either a feature-sliced layout (code split into ordered layers, each split into slices by feature or business area, where code in a slice may import from its own slice and from lower layers, never from another slice of its own layer, and reaches another slice only through that slice's public entry point) or a layered src directory (where a layer imports only from the layers it is built on); and whether one package imports another package's internal files instead of its public entry point (a deep import).

current: Reproducible, pinned builds (SSDF PW.4 / SLSA): dependency lockfiles + the deny-by-default egress sandbox the build runs in (it can fetch only from allow-listed registries — build-time provenance). Advisory; never scored.
proposed: Whether the repository pins its dependencies: for each ecosystem it uses (one with a package manifest in the repository), whether the dependency versions are fixed in a committed file, either a lockfile or one shared file fixing the versions for every project of that ecosystem (for example .NET's central package management), so that a build resolves the same versions every time. Evidence toward practice PW.4 of the NIST SSDF (Secure Software Development Framework) and toward SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts). Pinning committed in the repository does not prove that the build uses it, that the build is reproducible bit for bit, or that it reaches any SLSA level. Advisory: reported, never scored.

current: Whether async methods accept a CancellationToken so work can be cancelled (adoption curve).
proposed: Whether asynchronous methods in production code accept a cancellation token or signal (for example a CancellationToken in .NET or an AbortSignal in JavaScript), so their work can be cancelled (adoption curve). Methods whose signature a framework fixes (for example overrides or UI event handlers) are not counted unless they take one. Accepting one does not show that it is passed on to the work the method starts or honoured there.

current: Whether nullable reference types are enabled and not undermined by heavy `!` suppression.
proposed: Whether C# nullable reference types (the compiler's checks that a reference may be null) are enabled for the code (for example by a project setting or a `#nullable enable` directive), and not undermined by heavy use of the null-forgiving operator (`!`), which silences those checks.

current: Whether JSON/XML is parsed with regex/string hacks while a real parser is already referenced in the same project — a classic source of silent data bugs.
proposed: Whether JSON or XML text is parsed by hand with regular expressions or string operations (for example pulling a value out by matching its key or tag), while a dedicated parser for that same format (for example a parsing library, or the language's standard-library module) is already referenced in the same project or build unit (for example a package or module), as a dependency or by an import in its code: a common source of silent data bugs.

current: Whether any `||`/`&&` operand logically implies another in the same chain, making it dead — the expression means something wider (or narrower) than it reads.
proposed: Whether, in a chain of conditions joined by logical or (`||`) or logical and (`&&`), one operand logically implies another, so one of them can never change the chain's value (under or, the operand that implies the other adds nothing; under and, the implied one restricts nothing): the condition tests less than it reads, which usually means a different condition was intended.

current: Whether one non-trivial boolean expression is written out character-identically in two or more files — a single-line clone the token-window duplication detector cannot see.
proposed: Whether one non-trivial boolean expression (at least 40 characters long, whitespace aside) is written out the same, character for character apart from whitespace, in two or more files: a copy too short for Code Duplication (D4) to count.

current: Whether any branch is dead by construction — a switch arm whose label can never equal a case-normalised subject, or an `else if` whose predicate the arm above has already swallowed.
proposed: Whether any branch is dead by construction, that is, can never run whatever the input, from the code alone: a switch label that can never equal the switch's subject because the code converts the subject to one letter case and the label has letters in the other case (for example an upper-case or mixed-case label against a lower-cased subject); or an else-if arm whose condition can be true only when the condition of an earlier arm in the same chain is also true, so every input that would satisfy it is already taken by that earlier arm (for example an earlier test that a string contains "ab" before a later test that it contains "abc"). An arm that only partly overlaps an earlier one is not dead. Not a general dead-code or coverage measure.

current: Whether a loop that shortens a string until it fits a length budget has a floor — one with none grinds the value down to the empty string, or past it into a negative-length `Substring`.
proposed: Whether a loop that shortens a string until it fits a length budget (the greatest length the string may have) has a floor: anything that ends the shortening no later than when the string is empty, in the loop condition or as a guard or exit (a break, return or throw) in its body. A direct comparison of the string's own length with the budget (for example length greater than the budget) is a floor, and so is a test that the string is not empty. A comparison in which the string's length is only one term is not a floor when the other terms alone can exceed the budget (for example its length plus a suffix's length compared with the budget, where the suffix alone can be longer than the budget). A loop with no floor grinds the value down to the empty string and then past it: into a substring request with a negative length, which fails at run time in some languages, or, where the language clamps it, a loop that never ends.

current: Whether a walk that recurses through a JSON/XML tree handed in by its caller bounds how deep it will go — an uncapped walk lets the document's nesting choose the stack depth, and the resulting StackOverflowException cannot be caught.
proposed: Whether a walk that recurses through a JSON or XML tree handed in by its caller bounds how deep it will go (for example with a depth or remaining-levels value carried through each recursive call): an uncapped walk lets the document's nesting choose the stack depth, and the resulting stack overflow in some runtimes (for example .NET) cannot be caught and ends the process.

current: Whether an argument guard throws the exception its own condition describes — a guard that rejects a value for being EMPTY and reports it as `ArgumentNullException` tells the caller a parameter was null when it provably was not.
proposed: Whether an argument guard throws the exception its own condition describes: a guard that rejects a value for being empty and reports it as a null argument (for example ArgumentNullException in .NET, or a type derived from it) tells the caller a parameter was null when it provably was not.

current: Whether a `when` guard is free of side effects — a guard that increments a counter or assigns while deciding whether its arm matches applies that change during PATTERN MATCHING, on an arm that may not be selected, and skips it entirely when a short-circuit to its left answers first.
proposed: Whether a pattern-match guard (in C#, the `when` clause of a switch case or switch-expression arm) is free of side effects: a guard that increments, decrements or assigns while deciding whether its arm matches applies that change during pattern matching, on an arm that may not be selected, and skips it entirely when it sits where a short-circuiting operator in the guard can skip it (the right operand of and, or or null-coalescing, a branch of a conditional, or after a null-conditional access) and that operator answers first.

current: Whether a method that TAKES a lock or semaphore and gives it back from a flag-guarded `finally` returns the value that flag implies — reporting success while the guard hands the primitive back admits a second caller the exclusion was there to keep out, and reporting failure while the guard keeps it leaves nothing to ever give it back.
proposed: Whether a method that itself takes a lock or semaphore, and gives it back in an always-run cleanup block (for example `finally`) only as a true/false flag directs, returns a success or failure result that agrees with the flag's state at that return: success means the caller still holds the lock or semaphore, failure means the cleanup gives it back. A mismatch either lets a second caller past the exclusion or leaves the lock or semaphore held with nothing to ever give it back.

current: Whether the work a diagnostic log line costs is paid only when that line is wanted — C# evaluates a call's arguments BEFORE the call, so a trace/debug message joined or projected out of a collection is built in full on every pass, and then discarded by a sink the shipped configuration leaves switched off.
proposed: Whether, in production code (tests excluded), the work a diagnostic log line costs is paid only when that line is wanted: where a call's arguments are evaluated before the call, a trace, debug or verbose message whose arguments do work that scales with a collection (for example joining, projecting or serialising it) is built in full every time the call runs, and then discarded by a level the shipped configuration leaves switched off, unless the work is deferred into a function the logger calls only when the level is on, or a check of the log level, a build switch or conditional compilation keeps it from running.

current: Whether a value the caller is invited to supply is the value the type actually uses — a constructor parameter stored in a private field that nothing ever reads while the default it was given is spelled out a second time at the site that should have read it, a keyed lookup that falls back to a different setting than the one its key names while the same type falls back to the matching one for that same key, or a culture-sensitive parse given no format provider by a type that feeds its own settable culture to the same kind of parse elsewhere. Either way, every caller who supplies a value silently gets something else.
proposed: Whether a value the caller is invited to supply is the value the type actually uses: a constructor parameter stored in a private field that nothing reads, while the default it was given is written out again where the field should have been read; a lookup by key that falls back to a different setting than the one its key names, while elsewhere the same type falls back to the matching setting for that same key; or a culture-sensitive parse given no culture by a type that passes its own settable culture to the same kind of parse elsewhere. In each case a value someone supplies is silently replaced by another.

current: Whether a value handed from a callback to the body that waits on it crosses on something built to be crossed — a `Queue<T>`/`List<T>`/`Dictionary<K,V>` written inside an event handler and read back outside it is mutated by two flows at once, and the semaphore or completion source beside it orders how MANY items exist while leaving the collection's own head, tail and backing array unprotected.
proposed: Whether a value handed from a callback (for example an event handler) to the code waiting on it is passed through a structure made for concurrent use, under a lock, or otherwise without the callback and the outside code touching the same collection at overlapping times. A collection not made for concurrent use (for example a plain queue, list or dictionary) that the callback changes and that is also accessed outside the callback while the callback can still run is used by both at the same time. A semaphore, completion object or other wait handle beside it orders what the callback wrote before raising it, but does not protect an outside access that a run of the callback can overlap, including one made before the code waits for the run in progress; an outside access that no run of the callback can overlap (for example after the waiting code has observed the callback's final signal, when the callback no longer touches the collection after signalling) is not this.

current: Whether a `foreach` leaves the collection it is walking alone — a body that adds to or removes from the very collection the loop is enumerating invalidates the enumerator it is holding, so the next `MoveNext` throws `InvalidOperationException` and the remaining items are never seen.
proposed: Whether a C# `foreach` leaves the collection it is walking alone: a body that adds to or removes from the very collection the loop is enumerating invalidates the enumerator the loop holds, so the next `MoveNext` throws `InvalidOperationException` and the remaining items are never seen. Collections whose enumerator survives such a change (for example concurrent or immutable collections, and arrays), and a change the loop exits straight after, are not this.

current: Whether a condition that tests a value for emptiness indexes that same value only where the test holds — an `||` written one parenthesis too far to the left leaves an index access outside the guard beside it, so the empty case the guard exists to anticipate reaches the index and throws instead.
proposed: Whether a condition that tests a value for emptiness (for example a null-or-empty check, a length or count compared with a constant, or an any-element check) indexes that same value only where the test has established that it is not empty: for example, an or placed one parenthesis too far to the left can leave one index access outside the guard while another stays inside it, so the empty case the guard exists to anticipate reaches the index and fails.

current: Whether a guard written as a NEGATED `||` says what its author meant — `!(a || b || x != k)` is `!a && !b && x == k` by De Morgan, so a bail-out that mixes capabilities the code needs with a fault it refuses turns inside out: it fires only where the capabilities are ABSENT, and lets every value the fault term names walk straight into the body that cannot handle it.
proposed: Whether a guard written as the negation of a logical OR of two or more terms, which mixes capabilities the code needs (for example true/false flags) with a fault it refuses (for example a test that a value is not equal to a constant), says what its author meant. By De Morgan's law the negation of an OR is the AND of the negated terms, so, for example, `!(a || b || x != k)` with `k` a constant means `!a && !b && x == k`: an early-exit guard (one that leaves before the code it protects) turns inside out, firing only where every capability is absent and the value equals the constant, and letting every value the fault term was meant to refuse (here every x other than k) into the code that cannot handle it, whatever the capabilities. A negated OR whose terms are all capabilities or all faults is not this; a finding marks logic that contradicts the guard's evident intent, not a confirmed runtime failure.

current: Whether a production module publishes functions that exist only for its tests — Erlang has no visibility below `-export`, so a test helper exported unconditionally becomes part of the module's contract for every caller in the system, and the `-ifdef(TEST)` idiom that would keep it out of the shipped module is not used.
proposed: Whether an Erlang production module publishes functions that exist only for its tests: Erlang has no visibility below `-export`, so a test helper exported unconditionally becomes part of the module's contract for every caller in the system, instead of being exported inside an `-ifdef(TEST)` section that keeps it out of the shipped module.

current: Whether a plugin lookup names the type it means — searching every assembly loaded into the process for a candidate whose SIMPLE name equals a string supplied at runtime, and taking the first one found, is decided by assembly LOAD ORDER rather than by this source, so the same name can resolve to a different type on the next run.
proposed: Whether a plugin lookup names the type it means: searching the types of every assembly loaded into the process for one whose simple name (without its namespace) equals a string supplied at run time, and taking the first one found, is decided by the order the assemblies were loaded rather than by the source, so the same name can resolve to a different type on the next run. A lookup that requires exactly one match, or that requires the full name (with its namespace) to match as well as the simple name, is not this; one that accepts either name still is.
